=== av1-and-vp9
     1	---
     2	title: "AV1 and VP9"
     3	description: "Export delivery files and web movies with Frame Job's built-in AV1 and VP9 encoders, and know how their rates, time and memory behave."
     4	---
     5	
     6	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
     7	
     8	AV1 and VP9 aim to match or beat HEVC's picture at the same rate, and their WebM formats are for the web. Frame Job has their encoders built in, SVT-AV1 and libvpx, and they run in software.
     9	
    10	<AtAGlance
    11	  where={['Export sheet ▸ Format', 'Export sheet ▸ Speed (AV1 only)']}
    12	  tools="export"
    13	/>
    14	
    15	| Format | File | Sound | Picture | Keeps transparency | Can carry HDR | **Speed:** |
    16	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    17	| [AV1 (MP4)](#av1-mp4) | `.mp4` | AAC | 10-bit | No | Yes | Yes |
    18	| [AV1 (WebM)](#av1-webm) | `.webm` | Opus | 10-bit | No | Yes | Yes |
    19	| [VP9 (WebM)](#vp9-webm) | `.webm` | Opus | 8-bit, or 10-bit with HDR | No | Yes | Greyed out |
    20	| [VP9 with Alpha (WebM)](#vp9-with-alpha-webm) | `.webm` | Opus | 8-bit | Yes | No | Greyed out |
    21	
    22	All four write a keyframe at least every 2 seconds and need even dimensions, so an odd width or height is written one pixel smaller. All four write [chapters](/export/chapters/). The sheet [estimates the time](/export/export-sheet/#estimated-time) before you start.
    23	
    24	## AV1 (MP4)
    25	
    26	This is AV1 video and AAC sound in an MP4, for delivery. It's always 10-bit.
    27	
    28	**Speed:** offers **Faster**, **Balanced** and **Smaller file**, with **Balanced** the default. See [Encoder speed](/export/encoder-speed/). Slower settings take longer and write a smaller file.
    29	
    30	It encodes at a constant quality matched to HEVC, with the rate as a [soft cap](#the-rate-as-a-soft-cap). It's one of the six formats that can carry HDR. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).
    31	
    32	An M1 or M2 Mac can't [play the file back](#playback-on-m1-and-m2-macs).
    33	
    34	## AV1 (WebM)
    35	
    36	The same AV1 picture in a WebM file, for the web. It has the same encoder, speeds, soft cap and HDR as AV1 (MP4). Only the container and the sound differ.
    37	
    38	The sound is Opus, 48 kHz stereo, at 192 kbps unless a [Quality tier](/export/quality/) says otherwise, and it snaps to the nearest rate the encoder offers. A project with no sound exports a WebM with no sound track.
    39	
    40	## VP9 (WebM)
    41	
    42	VP9 in a WebM file with Opus sound, for the web. It has one speed, so **Speed:** is greyed out.
    43	
    44	An SDR picture is 8-bit, in VP9's Profile 0. HDR is 10-bit, in Profile 2. VP9 can't name HLG or PQ itself, so the WebM file tells the player which one it is. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).
    45	
    46	## VP9 with Alpha (WebM)
    47	
    48	VP9 (WebM) that keeps a transparent canvas, for a title or lower third a web page plays over its own background in Chrome or Firefox. Safari's transparent movie is [HEVC with Alpha (MOV)](/export/h264-and-hevc/#hevc-with-alpha-mov).
    49	
    50	- The picture is 8-bit, with the transparency as a second stream beside it. The [footnote](/export/export-sheet/#the-footnote) ends in `alpha`.
    51	- It's SDR only, so an HDR project writes its SDR version, and **Dynamic Range:** stays greyed out on **SDR version**.
    52	- The sound is Opus, as in VP9 (WebM).
    53	- A **Custom…** size of a different shape from the canvas won't export, because padding would lose the alpha. After the save panel the export stops with a message naming the canvas's size. Every row in the **Size:** popup is fine.
    54	- Imported back into Frame Job it shows opaque, because the transparency isn't read. For a transparent clip to bring back in, export ProRes 4444 or HEVC with Alpha.
    55	
    56	## The rate as a soft cap
    57	
    58	On AV1 and VP9 the video rate isn't a target. They encode at a constant quality chosen to match or beat HEVC at that rate, and the file usually stays under it. That's why the Quality tiers and the footnote read `usually ≤ …`.
    59	
    60	- With **Format default** the cap is HEVC's rate. With a tier it's 60 % of the H.264 rate, as for HEVC. See [Export quality](/export/quality/).
    61	- Simple footage comes out smaller than the rate.
    62	- Very detailed footage can go over it.
    63	- In an HDR export, VP9 matches HEVC 10-bit at that rate.
    64	- You can't know the file size in advance.
    65	
    66	On VP9 with Alpha the rate is the picture's alone. The transparency is a second stream at a fixed quality on top of it, so the file is larger than the rate says.
    67	
    68	## Memory and the queue
    69	
    70	A job in the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) waits while the AV1 and VP9 exports already running would use more than a quarter of the Mac's memory with it. Its row says why, for example "Waiting for memory: AV1 and VP9 exports running now hold about 6.0 GB of the 8.0 GB this Mac allows them, and this one needs about 3.0 GB." A later job may run first meanwhile.
    71	
    72	A job always starts when no other AV1 or VP9 export is running. **Export…** never waits, so starting several at once behind their progress sheets can go past that quarter. The memory each job needs is a measured figure, not a guarantee.
    73	
    74	## Playback on M1 and M2 Macs
    75	
    76	M1 and M2 Macs have no AV1 decoder, so Frame Job can't play or re-import an AV1 file there, MP4 or WebM. An import stops with a message saying the file needs an M3 or later Mac. The Mac can still export one.
    77	
    78	A VP9 (WebM) file re-imports on any Apple silicon Mac.
    79	
    80	## Good to know
    81	
    82	An AV1 rate is held at 100 Mbps at most.
    83	
    84	## Related
    85	
    86	- [Encoder speed](/export/encoder-speed/)
    87	- [Export quality](/export/quality/)
    88	- [Transparent exports](/export/transparency/)
    89	- [The Export Queue](/export/export-queue/)
=== gif-and-apng
     1	---
     2	title: "Animated GIF and PNG"
     3	description: "Export a short silent loop as an Animated GIF or Animated PNG, and keep it inside the size and the 600-frame limit."
     4	---
     5	
     6	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
     7	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
     8	
     9	GIF and APNG are for short silent loops you can send or drop into a page. Each stores every frame as a whole picture, so a long or large one quickly becomes a file nobody can send. That's why both start small and hold at most 600 frames.
    10	
    11	<AtAGlance
    12	  where="Export sheet ▸ Format"
    13	  tools="export"
    14	/>
    15	
    16	## Export a loop
    17	
    18	<Steps>
    19	
    20	1. Set an [in/out range](/timeline/in-out-range/) around the moment you want.
    21	
    22	2. Press <kbd>⌘E</kbd>, and choose **Animated GIF** or **Animated PNG** from **Format:**.
    23	
    24	3. Set **Range:** to **In/out range**.
    25	
    26	4. Check the readout, which shows the size and the frame count, such as `· 360 frames, no audio`.
    27	
    28	5. Choose **Export…**.
    29	
    30	</Steps>
    31	
    32	## Animated GIF
    33	
    34	A GIF is a short, silent `.gif` that loops forever. It starts at 480 × 270 and 12.5 fps, and you can still change the size and the rate.
    35	
    36	The 12.5 is deliberate. A GIF stores each frame's delay in hundredths of a second, so only rates that divide 100 play back exactly. 25 and 50 fps from the **Frame rate:** popup do too, and any other rate lands wherever the format's rounding puts it.
    37	
    38	A GIF has a palette of 256 colours. It can show a pixel as fully transparent but has no partial transparency, so soft edges go hard, and it isn't one of the [formats that keep transparency](/export/transparency/).
    39	
    40	## Animated PNG
    41	
    42	An APNG is a lossless, silent, true-colour `.png` that loops forever. It starts at 960 × 540 and 25 fps, and you can still change the size and the rate.
    43	
    44	It keeps real transparency, so a pixel can be any fraction of opaque, and the [footnote](/export/export-sheet/#the-footnote) ends in `alpha`. It's written at 8 bits a component and labelled BT.709.
    45	
    46	A viewer that knows nothing of APNG shows the first frame.
    47	
    48	## The 600-frame limit
    49	
    50	An animated GIF or APNG holds at most 600 frames. That's 48 seconds at GIF's 12.5 fps, or 24 seconds at APNG's 25 fps. The readout shows the count while you're choosing, but the sheet doesn't stop you. Once you've picked where to save, a longer export stops before it writes anything:
    51	
    52	> An animated GIF is limited to 600 frames and this range is 720. Shorten the range, or lower the export frame rate.
    53	
    54	For GIF the way out is a shorter range, because every fixed rate in the **Frame rate:** popup is higher than 12.5 fps. An APNG can go down to 24 or 23.976 fps, which gains you about a second.
    55	
    56	## Fitting inside the size
    57	
    58	The **Size:** popup lists **GIF default** or **APNG default** first, and it's the default for those two formats and no others. Each is 480 × 270 or 960 × 540, fitted to the canvas's shape.
    59	
    60	Every row, and a **Custom…** size, is a box the picture fits inside. It keeps its shape and is never enlarged, and nothing is letterboxed. The rows show the size the file will have. A 1080 × 1920 project's GIF default is 152 × 270.
    61	
    62	Because the picture is never enlarged, rows bigger than the canvas come out as the canvas's own size, and the popup hides rows that repeat an earlier row's numbers. An odd width or height is kept.
    63	
    64	## Good to know
    65	
    66	- **Quality:** and **Loudness:** are greyed out, and so are **Bit depth:** and **Stems:**. Neither format has a bit rate or any sound.
    67	- **Burn in timecode** still works.
    68	- Neither format has [chapters](/export/chapters/).
    69	- Both write the SDR version in an HDR project.
    70	
    71	## Related
    72	
    73	- [Choose a format](/export/formats/)
    74	- [Export a range](/export/range/)
    75	- [Export size](/export/size/)
    76	- [Export frame rate](/export/frame-rate/)

---
title: "Export: start, then poll"
description: Write a file from an agent, follow the job until it finishes, stop it, and read what the file holds.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

An agent's export doesn't wait for the file. `export` checks the request, puts a job on the Export Queue and answers at once, and the agent then asks how it's going until it ends.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['File ▸ Export…', 'Window ▸ Export Queue']}
  keys="⌘E"
  where="The export sheet's Add to Queue, and each row's Cancel in the Export Queue"
  tools={['export', 'export_status', 'cancel_export']}
/>

## Write a file

<Steps>

1. Call `export` with a preset and a path. It answers straight away.

   ```json
   { "preset": "h264", "path": "/Volumes/Edits/cut", "size": "1080p" }
   ```

   ```json
   { "export_id": 3, "path": "/Volumes/Edits/cut.mp4", "status": "running" }
   ```

2. Call `export_status` with that `export_id`, pause, and call it again until `status` is `done`, `failed` or `cancelled`.

3. Read the `done` answer. It says what the file holds, including the loudness it measured and any warnings.

</Steps>

To stop the job, call `cancel_export`. The job shows in **Window ▸ Export Queue** like any other, but the window doesn't open by itself.

## Export

`export` does what **File ▸ Export…** does with **Add to Queue**, and it runs through the same writer, so an agent's file and a person's match. It takes the [export sheet](/export/export-sheet/)'s controls in the sheet's own terms, apart from the frame rate.

| Argument | Type | Required | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `preset` | string | Yes | The encoding: a container and a codec. See [Presets](#presets). |
| `path` | string | Yes | Where to write, such as `~/Movies/cut.mp4`. See [Path handling](#path-handling). |
| `size` | string or `[width, height]` | No | The output size. See [Size](#size). |
| `range` | string | No | `project` for the whole timeline, or `in_out` for the in and out range. See [Range](#range). |
| `video_bitrate` | integer | No | Target video rate in bits per second. See [Exact bitrates](#exact-bitrates). |
| `audio_bitrate` | integer | No | Target AAC or Opus rate in bits per second. See [Exact bitrates](#exact-bitrates). |
| `loudness_lufs` | number | No | Normalise the whole mix to this loudness, −70 to 0. See [The loudness report](#the-loudness-report). |
| `peak_dbtp` | number | No | The master limiter's ceiling, −20 to 0. See [Peak dBTP](#peak-dbtp). |
| `audio_bits` | integer | No | 16 or 24, for WAV and AIFF. See [Audio bits](#audio-bits). |
| `stems` | string | No | `tracks` or `names`, to write stems beside an audio mix. See [Stems](#stems). |
| `burn_in_timecode` | boolean | No | Draw the project timecode over the picture, on top of everything. Off by default. See [Burn in timecode](/export/burn-in-timecode/). |
| `dynamic_range` | string | No | `hlg`, `pq` or `sdr`, in an HLG project. See [Dynamic range](#dynamic-range). |
| `encoder_speed` | string | No | `faster`, `balanced` or `smaller`, for AV1. See [Encoder speed](#encoder-speed). |
| `project` | string | No | The path of the open project to export, as `get_project` reports it. Without it, the frontmost project. |

It answers `{export_id, path, status}`. `path` is the file that will be written, with `~` expanded and the extension corrected. `status` is `running` if the job started at once, or `queued` if it's waiting.

Jobs in the queue run one at a time, behind anything already there. A job writes the project as it stood when `export` was called, so later edits don't reach it. Calling `export` pauses playback in that project's window.

`export` takes no `scope`. With a [nest](/mcp/nests/) open it still writes the project's timeline, not the nest's.

## Export status

`export_status` answers how a job is going, as its row in the Export Queue would, and it never waits. Pass the `export_id`, which is an integer of 1 or more.

Every answer carries `export_id`, `status`, `path` and `elapsed`, the seconds since `export` was called, or from then to the finish once the job has ended. The rest depends on the status.

| `status` | Also carries |
| --- | --- |
| `queued` | `waiting` while an AV1 or VP9 job is held for memory. `estimated_seconds` on `av1`, `av1_webm`, `vp9_webm` and `vp9_alpha_webm`. |
| `running` | `progress`, from 0 to 1. `phase` while the export names one, which is "Measuring loudness…" during the first pass over the mix. `estimated_seconds` on the same four presets. |
| `done` | What the file holds, in the next table. |
| `failed` | `reason`, the queue row's sentence. |
| `cancelled` | `reason`, the queue row's sentence. |

`estimated_seconds` is the export sheet's estimate of the whole export in whole seconds, and it's only an estimate.

`waiting` is a sentence such as "Waiting for memory: AV1 and VP9 exports running now hold about 2.1 GB of the 8.0 GB this Mac allows them, and this one needs about 7.0 GB." AV1 and VP9 exports may hold a quarter of this Mac's memory between them, though a job with no other running always starts. While one is held, a later job in the queue may run first.

A `done` answer adds these keys.

| Key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `ok` | `true`. |
| `bytes` | The file's size. |
| `preset`, `container`, `codec` | What was written. |
| `width`, `height` | The file's size in pixels. These are reported on audio presets too, where they mean nothing. |
| `fps` | The rate as `[num, den]`, such as `[30, 1]`. |
| `start`, `duration` | The part of the timeline written, in [ticks](/mcp/units-and-ids/). |
| `burn_in_timecode` | Whether the argument was on. |
| `dynamic_range` | The picture written: `hlg`, `pq` or `sdr`. Only for a video preset in an HLG project. |
| `encoder_speed` | The speed used. Only on `av1` and `av1_webm`. |
| `audio_bits` | The depth written. Only on `audio_wav` and `audio_aiff`. |
| `stems` | `[{name, tracks, path}]`, one per file beside the mix. Only when `stems` was asked for. |
| `loudness` | What the mix measured. See [The loudness report](#the-loudness-report). |
| `graphic_warnings` | `[{name, frame, message}]`, each distinct warning a graphic gave while the file was drawn. Collecting stops after 64 distinct reports, so a noisy graphic's list can be cut short. `frame` is the graphic's own frame, or `null`. Absent when there were none. |
| `cursor_warnings` | `[{media, path, message}]`, each media whose cursor file couldn't be drawn. Its clips were written without a cursor. Absent when there were none. |

## Cancel export

`cancel_export` stops a job, as the row's **Cancel** does, and answers as `export_status` does. Pass the `export_id`.

| The job is | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Queued | It's cancelled before it starts. The answer reads `cancelled`, with the reason "Cancelled before it started." |
| Running | It stops and its half-written file is removed. The answer may still read `running` until the writer has stopped, and `export_status` then reads `cancelled`, with the reason "Cancelled." |
| Finished | It's left alone, and its file stays. The answer is the finished job's. |

## Export id and its lifetime

An `export_id` is known until Frame Job quits. Removing a finished row from the Export Queue, or choosing **Clear Finished**, doesn't lose it, so an agent can still read how that job ended.

An id belongs to the launch, not to a project, so `export_status` and `cancel_export` don't need `project`. Only ids that `export` answered are known. A job a person queued from the sheet has no id an agent can follow. Any other number answers "No export this launch has export_id 7 — ids come from export and last until Frame Job quits."

## Refusals and failures

A problem Frame Job can see from the request comes back from `export` itself as an error, and nothing is queued.

| The request | What stops it |
| --- | --- |
| An empty timeline | "There is nothing on the timeline to export." |
| A folder that doesn't exist | "There is no folder at … to write into." Frame Job never creates the folder. |
| An unknown preset | The error lists all the presets. |
| An unknown `size`, or one it can't read | The error lists the sizes. See [Size](#size). |
| `range` of `in_out` with no range set | "This project has no in/out range — set one with set_range `{start, end}`, or export with range \"project\"." |
| A number out of range, or a word it doesn't know | The error names the argument and the value. |
| An option the preset doesn't have | See [Audio bits](#audio-bits), [Stems](#stems), [Dynamic range](#dynamic-range) and [Encoder speed](#encoder-speed). |
| A graphic clip in the range with no module, or a module that doesn't compile | "The export was not started: the graphic "…" does not compile — …. Fix the module and export again." A clip with no module reads "has no module in graphics/" in place of "does not compile — …". It names each graphic and its first error, and it covers graphics inside nests. An audio-only preset draws no graphics, so it isn't stopped by one. |

Anything that goes wrong after that comes back from `export_status` as `failed`, with the sentence in `reason`. Check for it even when `export` answered cleanly.

| What went wrong | The `reason` |
| --- | --- |
| A size of another shape on a transparent preset | "An export that keeps transparency has to have the canvas's own shape…". See [Transparent presets](#transparent-presets). |
| A stem's file would be one of the project's media | "The stem “…” would replace media this project uses; export under another name." |
| A graphic fails while it's drawn | "The export was stopped at frame … of the graphic "…": …. No file was written." |
| A retimed clip's sound, an isolated voice or a voice effect couldn't be rendered | The sentence names the clip and the reason. |
| A cut-out clip's masks couldn't be made | "Clip …'s person masks could not be made: …." A picture cut out by **Foreground** says foreground masks. |
| A clip's gate, leveller or de-esser needs a loudness that hasn't been measured | "Clip …'s loudness or speech has not been measured yet…". Wait for the clip's analysis, then export again. |
| This Mac has no encoder for the preset | "This Mac cannot export with the “…” preset." |

A graphic's warnings are different: they don't stop the export, and they arrive as `graphic_warnings` in the `done` answer.

## Presets

There are 15 presets, one per encoding. A preset says nothing about size. These are the rows of the sheet's **Format** control, described in [Choose a format](/export/formats/). A wrong id's error lists them all.

| Preset | In the sheet | File | Picture | Sound |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `h264` | H.264 (MP4) | `.mp4` | 8-bit. The sheet's first row. | AAC |
| `hevc` | HEVC (MP4) | `.mp4` | 8-bit | AAC |
| `hevc_alpha` | HEVC with Alpha (MOV) | `.mov` | 8-bit with transparency. Safari's transparent movie. | AAC |
| `hevc_10bit` | HEVC 10-bit (MP4) | `.mp4` | 10-bit | AAC |
| `av1` | AV1 (MP4) | `.mp4` | 10-bit | AAC |
| `av1_webm` | AV1 (WebM) | `.webm` | 10-bit | Opus |
| `vp9_webm` | VP9 (WebM) | `.webm` | 8-bit for an SDR picture, 10-bit for HLG and PQ. One speed. | Opus |
| `vp9_alpha_webm` | VP9 with Alpha (WebM) | `.webm` | Always 8-bit, with transparency. The transparent movie Chrome and Firefox play. | Opus |
| `prores_422` | ProRes 422 (MOV) | `.mov` | 10-bit. An editing master. | 16-bit LPCM |
| `prores_4444` | ProRes 4444 (MOV) | `.mov` | 12-bit with transparency. A master. | 16-bit LPCM |
| `audio_m4a` | Audio only (M4A) | `.m4a` | None | AAC |
| `audio_wav` | Audio only (WAV) | `.wav` | None | 48 kHz LPCM, 16 or 24 bits |
| `audio_aiff` | Audio only (AIFF) | `.aiff` | None | 48 kHz LPCM, 16 or 24 bits |
| `gif` | Animated GIF | `.gif` | 256 colours. Fits inside 480 × 270 unless `size` says otherwise. | None |
| `apng` | Animated PNG | `.png` | Lossless, with transparency. Fits inside 960 × 540 unless `size` says otherwise. | None |

Macs before M3 can't play `av1` and `av1_webm` back.

## Frame rate

There's no frame-rate argument, so the sheet's [frame rate](/export/frame-rate/) control has no agent equivalent. An export runs at the project's rate, `gif` at 12.5 fps and `apng` at 25 fps. The `done` answer's `fps` says which, with 12.5 fps as `[25, 2]`.

## Path handling

The folder must exist. A `~` at the start is expanded, and an existing file at the path is replaced.

The file always ends in the preset's extension.

| `path` | `preset` | Writes | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `cut.mp4` | `h264` | `cut.mp4` | The extension is already right. |
| `cut` | `h264` | `cut.mp4` | With no extension, it's added. |
| `cut.mov` | `h264` | `cut.mp4` | A different media extension is replaced. |
| `Talk v1.2` | `h264` | `Talk v1.2.mp4` | Any other suffix stays part of the name. |
| `cut.webm` | `h264` | `cut.webm.mp4` | `.webm` isn't one of the extensions Frame Job replaces. |
| `cut.mp4` | `av1_webm` | `cut.webm` | `.mp4` is. |

The extensions it replaces are `.mov`, `.mp4`, `.m4v`, `.m4a`, `.mp3`, `.wav`, `.aif`, `.aiff`, `.caf`, `.framejob`, `.srt`, `.vtt`, `.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.heic` and `.gif`. The answer's `path` is always the file that gets written.

## Size

`size` is the sheet's **Size** control. See [Export size](/export/size/) for what the sizes mean to a person.

| `size` | In the sheet | What it writes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `document` | Document size | The project's own size. The default on every movie preset. |
| `2160p` | 4K | A short edge of 2160 pixels. |
| `1440p` | 1440p | A short edge of 1440 pixels. |
| `1080p` | 1080p | A short edge of 1080 pixels. |
| `720p` | 720p | A short edge of 720 pixels. |
| `preset` | GIF default, APNG default | The format's cap. `gif` and `apng` only, where it's the default. |
| `[width, height]` | Custom… | Exactly this size, from 16 to 8192 pixels on each edge. |

The number is always the short edge, and the long edge follows the project's shape, rounded to an even number. A vertical project's `1080p` is 1080 × 1920. Every size means the same on every project, so a 1920 × 1080 project's `1080p` is its own size, and a size larger than the project scales it up.

A movie is written at exactly the size asked for. If the shape differs from the project's by more than a pixel, the picture is letterboxed. Within a pixel, it fills the frame instead.

- **Even edges.** Every preset but `prores_4444`, `gif` and `apng` needs even dimensions, so an odd width or height is written one pixel smaller. That covers `document` on a project with an odd edge. The `done` answer's `width` and `height` are the file's.
- **GIF and APNG.** A size is a box the picture is fitted inside, keeping its shape and never scaling up. A vertical 1080 × 1920 project's GIF default comes out at 152 × 270.
- **Audio presets.** A size has no effect, and `preset` isn't one of their sizes.
- **Transparent movies.** A `[width, height]` of another shape fails. See [Transparent presets](#transparent-presets).

An unknown size answers with the list, for example "No export size is called "480p" for h264. The sizes are: document, 2160p, 1440p, 1080p, 720p — or pass [width, height]." A custom size outside 16 to 8192 pixels is turned down the same way, not clamped.

## Range

`range` is the sheet's **Range** control. `project`, the default, writes the whole timeline. `in_out` writes the range set with `set_range`, and it's turned down when there's no range. See [Export a range](/export/range/).

The range is snapped to the export's frame grid and kept inside the project. A range that comes to nothing is turned down.

`burn_in_timecode` shows project time even in a range export, so a file written from 00:00:10:00 begins at 00:00 with a burn-in that reads 00:00:10:00.

## Exact bitrates

The sheet offers [quality](/export/quality/) tiers. An agent sets the rates directly, in bits per second, so 8 Mbps is `8000000`. Each must be a whole number from 1 to 4,294,967,295.

`video_bitrate` is the target video rate. Without it, Frame Job works out a rate from the frame size and frame rate. ProRes, GIF and APNG ignore it, because ProRes is fixed by its profile and the other two have no bitrate.

On the AV1 and VP9 presets it works differently:

- **`av1` and `av1_webm`.** It's a soft cap. The encoder works at a constant quality matched to HEVC at that rate, and the file usually comes in well under it. Very detailed footage can go up to about 1.25 times over. Without it, the quality is matched to HEVC at 0.07 bits per pixel per frame.
- **`vp9_webm`.** It's a soft cap too, matched to HEVC, or HEVC 10-bit in an HDR export. Up to about 1.15 times over was measured.
- **`vp9_alpha_webm`.** It's the same soft cap on the picture's stream alone. The transparency's stream comes on top, at a constant quality.

`audio_bitrate` is the AAC or Opus rate, 192 kbps when absent. Opus takes the nearest rate its encoder offers. ProRes, WAV and AIFF ignore it, because they write LPCM.

## The loudness report

Every export with sound measures its own mix and reports it as `loudness` in the `done` answer, normalised or not. GIF and APNG have no sound, and a timeline with no sound has nothing to measure, so `loudness` is absent from both.

`loudness_lufs` normalises the whole mix to an integrated loudness, from −70 to 0. The sheet's [Loudness](/export/loudness/) rows are −14 for streaming, −16 for podcasts and −23 for EBU R 128 broadcast, and an agent can ask for any value, such as −14.5. The export measures itself first, then applies one gain to everything, through the master limiter. The file lands on the target with its loudest peaks limited, rather than the whole mix held down. GIF and APNG ignore it.

| Key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `summary` | The same line the queue row and the progress sheet show, such as "Peak −1.0 dBTP · −16.0 LUFS", with " · peaks limited by 8.6 dB" when the limiter took 0.05 dB or more. |
| `integrated_lufs` | The file's integrated loudness. Absent when it has none, and `summary` then says "loudness not measurable". |
| `true_peak_dbtp` | The file's true peak. `null` when it's silent. |
| `sample_peak_dbfs` | The file's sample peak, never above the true peak. `null` when it's silent. |
| `gain_db` | The gain applied to reach the target. |
| `ceiling_dbtp` | The master limiter's ceiling. |
| `limited_db` | How far the limiter turned the loudest peak down. |
| `capped_by_gain` | `true` when the +40 dB limit on the gain decided it, so the file may be short of the target. |
| `target_lufs` | The `loudness_lufs` asked for. Absent when none was. |

A programme shorter than one 400 ms measuring block, or one too quiet to pass the standard's gate, has a peak and no integrated loudness. Digital silence reads "Silent" in `summary`.

## Peak dBTP

Every export with sound goes through a master limiter, so the file's true peak stays at or under a ceiling. `peak_dbtp` sets that ceiling, from −20 to 0. It's −1 when absent, which is the sheet's fixed value. 0 is the loosest, and there's no way to turn the limiter off.

You can pass it with or without `loudness_lufs`. `limited_db` in the [report](#the-loudness-report) says how far the limiter turned the loudest peak down.

## Audio bits

`audio_bits` is the sheet's [Bit depth](/export/bit-depth/) control: 16, the default, or 24. It's rounded once from the mix and never dithered, and the `done` answer repeats it.

It works on `audio_wav` and `audio_aiff` only. On any other preset the answer is "h264 has no bit depth; audio_bits applies to audio_wav and audio_aiff", naming the preset. ProRes keeps 16-bit sound. Any other number is turned down whatever the preset.

## Stems

`stems` also writes [stems](/export/stems/) beside the mix, on `audio_m4a`, `audio_wav` and `audio_aiff`. It's the sheet's **Stems** control.

| `stems` | What it writes |
| --- | --- |
| `tracks` | One file per heard track. |
| `names` | One file per track name. Heard tracks whose names match, ignoring case, share a file, and an unnamed track gets its own. |

A track is heard when it has sound in it and isn't muted or silenced by another track's solo. Each stem is named `<file> - <track name>.<ext>`, beside the mix, so `mix.wav` and a track called Voice give `mix - Voice.wav`. An unnamed track is `Track N`, `/` and `:` in a name become `-`, and two stems that would share a name are told apart with ` (Track N)`.

A stem holds its tracks' sound before the master, with no loudness gain and no limiter, so the stems add up to the mix wherever the master changed nothing. Any file already at a stem's name is replaced.

The `done` answer lists each one as `stems [{name, tracks, path}]`. `tracks` holds the ids of the timeline tracks in that stem.

- On any other preset the answer is "h264 has no stems; stems applies to audio_m4a, audio_wav and audio_aiff", naming the preset.
- With no track heard, it's "stems: no track is heard, so there is no stem to write".
- If a stem's file would be one of the project's media, the job fails before any stem is written, and `export_status` gives the reason.
- A failed or cancelled job leaves neither the mix nor any stem behind.

## Dynamic range

`dynamic_range` chooses the picture an [HLG project](/hdr/dynamic-range/) writes. It's the sheet's **Dynamic Range** control.

| `dynamic_range` | What it writes |
| --- | --- |
| `hlg` | BT.2100 HLG, with no Dolby Vision. The default on the presets that carry HDR. |
| `pq` | HDR10: BT.2100 PQ at 1,000 cd/m², with a P3-D65 mastering display of 0.005–1,000 cd/m², MaxCLL 1,000 and MaxFALL 0. |
| `sdr` | The project's SDR version. |

The presets that carry HDR are `hevc_10bit`, `av1`, `av1_webm`, `vp9_webm`, `prores_422` and `prores_4444`. Every other video preset in an HLG project writes the SDR version, `vp9_alpha_webm` included, and audio presets ignore the argument.

- `hlg` or `pq` on another video preset answers "h264 is 8-bit and writes the SDR version; export dynamic_range "pq" as hevc_10bit, av1, av1_webm, vp9_webm, prores_422 or prores_4444".
- `hlg` or `pq` in an SDR project answers "dynamic_range "pq" needs an HLG project; set_canvas output "hlg" first".
- `sdr` in an SDR project changes nothing.

Once a job is `done`, `dynamic_range` in the answer names the picture that was written. An SDR project's answer has no such key.

## Encoder speed

`encoder_speed` trades export time for file size on `av1` and `av1_webm`. It's the sheet's [Speed](/export/encoder-speed/) control, and the `done` answer names the one used.

| `encoder_speed` | SVT-AV1 preset | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `faster` | 8 | The quickest. |
| `balanced` | 6 | The default. |
| `smaller` | 4 | The smallest file for the picture, and the slowest. |

On every other preset the answer is "h264 has no encoder speed; encoder_speed applies to av1 and av1_webm", naming the preset. That includes `vp9_webm` and `vp9_alpha_webm`, which have one speed.

## Transparent presets

Four presets keep a transparent canvas transparent: `prores_4444`, `hevc_alpha`, `vp9_alpha_webm` and `apng`. See [Transparent exports](/export/transparency/). A GIF can show a fully transparent pixel, but it has no alpha channel, so nothing partial survives.

On the three movie presets, a `[width, height]` of a different shape from the canvas can't be written, because the padding would destroy the alpha channel. `export` queues the job, and `export_status` then reads `failed` with a reason that names both sizes. The shape is judged after an odd edge is evened, and within a pixel the picture fills the frame, so a size in the canvas's own proportions always works, at any scale. Every named size already has the canvas's shape.

`apng` fits its picture inside the size instead, so this doesn't apply to it.

    /// The footnote over the buttons: the codec, the container, and the rates
    /// the CORE resolved — never the ones the tier asked for, and not filtered by
    /// what the sheet thinks applies, since a preset is free to carry a rate
    /// of its own that no control here offered.
    ///
    /// The distinction matters because `export.rs` drops override keys it
    /// does not know, silently (the same trap the range comment above names).
    /// A tier picked against a core that has no bit-rate overrides has to
    /// read as "the format's own rate" rather than let the popup imply a
    /// number the file will not have.
    private func footnoteText(for settings: ExportSettings) -> String {
        var parts = [settings.codec.uppercased()]
        let container = settings.container.uppercased()
        // A frame-sequence preset's codec IS its container: "GIF · GIF".
        if container != parts[0] { parts.append(container) }
        if let speed = settings.encoderSpeed { parts.append(speed.menuName) }
        if settings.audioBits == 24 { parts.append("24-bit") }
        if case let n = settings.stems.count, n > 0 { parts.append(n == 1 ? "1 stem" : "\(n) stems") }
        if let rate = settings.videoBitrate {
            // A bundled encoder's rate is a soft cap (spec §11 CX-13).
            parts.append((settings.writer == nil ? "" : "usually ≤ ") + Self.rateText(rate))
        }
        if let rate = settings.audioBitrate {
            parts.append("\(Self.rateText(rate)) audio")
        }
        if currentTier != nil, settings.videoBitrate == nil, settings.audioBitrate == nil {
            parts.append("format's own rate")
        }
        // The core's echo, not the popup's row: a build whose
        // `export_settings` has never heard of `loudness_lufs` drops the key
        // silently, and the footnote must not then promise a normalisation
        // the file will not have.
        if let target = settings.loudnessLufs {
            parts.append(
                String(format: "%g LUFS", target).replacingOccurrences(of: "-", with: "−"))
        }
        // Whether the ENCODING carries a fourth channel — the core's own
        // answer for this row (`ExportSettings.alpha`), never a reading of the
        // canvas. It is the one place the sheet says which format keeps a
        // transparent background, and it is a POSITIVE claim only: the rows
        // that answer false are not enumerated here, because the flag says
        // what the settings object says and the footnote's whole rule is that
        // it reports the core rather than the popup.
        if settings.alpha { parts.append("alpha") }
        return parts.joined(separator: " · ")
    }
}
